recommendations.improvement_summary_text: 50 mm internal or external wall insulation
recommendations.improvement_descr_text: Solid wall insulation involves adding a layer of insulation to either the inside or the outside surface of the external walls, which reduces heat loss and lowers fuel bills. As it is more expensive than cavity wall insulation it is only recommended for walls without a cavity, or where for technical reasons a cavity cannot be filled. Internal insulation, known as dry-lining, is where a layer of insulation is fixed to the inside surface of external walls; this type of insulation is best applied when rooms require redecorating and can be installed by a competent DIY enthusiast. External solid wall insulation is the application of an insulant and a weather-protective finish to the outside of the wall. This may improve the look of the home, particularly where existing brickwork or rendering is poor, and will provide long-lasting weather protection. Further information can be obtained from the National Insulation Association (www.nationalinsulationassociation.org.uk).

recommendations.improvement_summary_text: Replace single glazed windows with low-E double glazed windows
recommendations.improvement_descr_text: Double glazing is the term given to a system where two panes of glass are made up into a sealed unit. Replacing existing single-glazed windows with double-glazed windows will improve comfort in the home by reducing draughts and cold spots near windows. Double-glazed windows may also reduce noise, improve security and combat problems with condensation.

Insulation of a floor will significantly reduce heat loss; this will improve levels of comfort, reduce energy use and lower fuel bills. Suspended floors can often be insulated from below. . Further information about floor insulation is available from many sources including www.energysavingtrust.org.uk/northernireland/Insulation/Floor-insulation.

A solar PV system is one which converts light directly into electricity via panels placed on the roof with no waste and no emissions. This electricity is used throughout the home in the same way as the electricity purchased from an energy supplier. The British Photovoltaic Association has up-to-date information on local installers who are qualified electricians. It is best to obtain advice from a qualified electrician. Ask the electrician to explain the options.

Fitting draught proofing, strips of insulation around windows and doors, will improve the comfort in the home. A contractor can be employed but draught proofing can be installed by a competent DIY enthusiast.

grant.basis: User requested BUS deduction for this mains-gas replacement. Installer must confirm eligibility and voucher; not an award.

operatingAssumptions.pricingBasis: User-directed revision: halve all monetary installation allowances from the earlier prototype; retain 15% contingency. These are editable budget assumptions, not supplier prices.

sources.title: GOV.UK: BUS grant amounts
sources.basis: £7,500 air-to-water heat pump grant for the proposed mains-gas replacement, subject to eligibility.

sources.title: Energy Saving Trust: heat pump efficiency and operation
sources.basis: Supports seasonal efficiency and weather compensation concepts. The specific 45/50/55°C SPF values here are illustrative assumptions, not values published by this source.

limits: Annual space heat defaults to design kW × 1,600 equivalent full-load hours; a transparent rough proxy, not an audited annual simulation or EPC-derived demand. Edit annual useful heat when bills/occupancy support a better estimate.
27 p/kWh is an illustrative flat electricity rate, not a quoted tariff or annual price forecast. No solar or time-of-use saving is assumed.

Heating SPF assumptions 3.6 / 3.3 / 3.0 correspond to design flow 45 / 50 / 55°C with weather compensation. Flow is not assumed constant all year. Actual equipment, climate, cycling, defrost and commissioning change performance.

Hot water is separate: 3,000 kWh/year of heat including assumed cylinder losses, SPF 2.5, plus 150 kWh/year auxiliary/backup electricity outside those SPF assumptions. Neither is a measured household quantity.
Costs include electricity for space heating, hot water and the auxiliary allowance. Exclude standing charges, non-heating household electricity, servicing, finance and future tariff changes.
The sensitivity range varies useful heat ±25% and both SPFs ±15%, with auxiliary electricity fixed. It is a scenario range, not a statistical confidence interval.

BUS deduction is shown separately after installation contingency. Eligibility and grant confirmation remain open; switching it off restores the gross amount. No grant is counted as running-cost savings.
operatingAssumptions.radiatorPricingBasis: User instruction: £300 per radiator change, treated as supply and fitting before contingency; editable. Existing heating is assumed in occupied rooms. Unknown output does not imply absence, adequacy at heat-pump temperatures, or an automatic replacement.

emitters.title: Lower-ground column radiator
emitters.observation: About eight front sections are visible on the exposed brick wall. Bottom is cropped.
emitters.assumptions: Central guess: 8 sections, about 900 mm high, 3 columns deep (~394 mm wide). Compare 7–9 sections, 750–1000 mm, 2–4 columns. Brick/door scale is approximate; study assignment follows the earlier tentative lower-ground attribution.

emitters.title: Hall column radiator
emitters.observation: White tubular sections are visible; near end and lower edge extend beyond the photo.
emitters.assumptions: Central guess: 18 sections, 600 mm high, 3 columns (~854 mm wide). Plausible alternatives: 14 sections/600 mm/2 columns to 24 sections/750 mm/4 columns. Cropping limits the total count.

emitters.title: Living-room bay radiator
emitters.observation: A separate white column radiator is visible below the central bay window, behind the table and chair.
emitters.assumptions: Central guess: 24 sections, 600 mm high, 3 columns (~1130 mm wide), using the window span as a loose scale cue. Occlusion allows 20 sections/500 mm/2 columns to 30 sections/600 mm/4 columns. Dining photo is a repeat view, not another emitter.

emitters.title: Kitchen window radiator
emitters.observation: A narrow part of a white ribbed radiator is visible behind the table/chair below the window.
emitters.assumptions: Very weak dimensions: central panel hypothesis 600 x 600 mm, K1; alternatives 450 x 400 mm K1 to 600 x 800 mm K2. Panel versus tubular construction cannot be resolved; this is a broad output proxy. The second kitchen photo shows the same position.

emitters.title: Rear living-area panel radiator
emitters.observation: White ribbed panel below the side window, largely hidden by the chair and table; separate from the kitchen-window radiator.
emitters.assumptions: Central guess: 450 x 1000 mm K1. Compare 450 x 700 mm K1 to 600 x 1200 mm K2; width uses the window as an approximate reference. Rear photograph has no metric camera calibration for emitter sizing.

emitters.title: Front-bedroom bay radiator
emitters.observation: White tubular radiator beneath the central bay window, partly hidden by the chair.
emitters.assumptions: Front bay identifies Bedroom 1 more strongly than the listing caption alone. Central guess: 28 sections, 600 mm high, 3 columns (~1314 mm wide). Compare 22 sections/500 mm/2 columns to 32 sections/600 mm/4 columns.

emitters.title: Bathroom towel frame
emitters.observation: Brass-coloured open frame with a few horizontal rails and apparent valve connections, above the bath.
emitters.assumptions: Approximate 800 x 500 mm frame. Central 180 W DT50, bracket 120–300 W, using a 210 W 965 x 500 mm brass-frame analogue. Multipliers allow different dimensions/finish; this is a heuristic, not validated geometric scaling. Hot-water/electric connection and towel effects need checking.

emitters.title: Unassigned bedroom radiator
emitters.observation: White column radiator below a sash window beside the bed.
emitters.assumptions: Central guess: 14 sections/600 mm/3 columns (~670 mm wide). Compare 10 sections/500 mm/2 columns to 20 sections/750 mm/4 columns. Sloping ceiling suggests the rear bedroom, but attribution to Bedroom 2 versus 3 is unresolved; exclude from room totals.

unresolved.observation: Possible radiator behind the right-hand sofa, but upholstery and emitter edges are not reliably separable. Retain the original observation; no numeric estimate and no double counting with the bay radiator.

limits: Section counts run across the radiator; column counts describe front-to-back depth. Never confuse them.
All sizes are photo guesses. Source pixels are not metric measurements and are not independently rectified.
Photo inventories are partial. A shortfall for visible radiators cannot prove that the entire room requires replacements.
Manufacturer curves are analogues; the actual installed brands/models and hydronic connection remain unverified.
Photos with no visible emitter remain unknown; bathroom mirror reflections and repeat room views are not additional emitters.

emitters.observation: Partly obscured white radiator beneath kitchen window; depth and panel count not visible.

surveyTasks.why: The four photo observations are an incomplete inventory.
surveyTasks.method: Walk every room, including halls, bathrooms and lower ground; link each emitter or confirmed absence to a stable room ID.

surveyTasks.title: Locate meter, consumer unit and supply route
surveyTasks.why: Meter position alone does not establish a suitable electrical connection.
surveyTasks.method: Qualified electrical assessment: locate meter, service and consumer unit; record supply capacity, earthing, spare ways and a feasible protected cable route.

fields.label: Electrical assessor findings and remaining checks

surveyTasks.title: Locate existing hot-water equipment and cylinder options
surveyTasks.why: Cylinder volume, access, support and recovery requirements depend on the house and household.
surveyTasks.method: Identify existing system, available cupboard dimensions, delivery route, structural support, drainage and connections; ask about hot-water use.

fields.label: Occupancy and hot-water use; evidence source

surveyTasks.title: Measure outdoor siting options
surveyTasks.why: Usable ground, sound, airflow, servicing, drains and routing constrain location.
surveyTasks.method: Compare rear courtyard options with homeowners; measure available envelope and routes, drainage, neighbour receptors and obstacles. Check selected manufacturer and current applicable siting requirements.

fields.label: Clearances, noise, drainage, access and checks still required

surveyTasks.title: Trace hydraulic and electrical routes
surveyTasks.why: Straight-line distances miss walls, level changes, access and hydraulic resistance.
surveyTasks.method: Record separate route segments from outdoor unit to hydraulic/cylinder connections, heating circuit, consumer unit and condensate discharge. Mark length, vertical rise, diameter, fittings, penetrations and access.

fields.label: Endpoint IDs and measured route segments

surveyTasks.title: Record homeowner choices and constraints
surveyTasks.why: Layout and equipment changes need explicit household choices.
surveyTasks.method: Discuss comfort, rooms used, hot-water habits, refurbishment plans, outdoor space, cylinder storage trade-offs, radiator appearance and disruption. Record preferred alternatives separately from technical approval.

fields.label: Named option IDs, preferences and unresolved choices

options.title: Outdoor unit near rear courtyard
options.tradeoff: Potentially short route to rear kitchen; compare noise, airflow, garden use and service access.

options.title: Cylinder in lower-ground utility area
options.tradeoff: May preserve upstairs storage; access, headroom, support, drainage and route remain unknown.

options.title: Alternative internal cylinder space
options.tradeoff: Survey other cupboards; compare delivery access, storage loss and connection distances.

limits: Sensitivity scenarios, not confidence intervals or equipment selections.
Room areas include wall/void uncertainty; upper rear room ceiling heights are especially uncertain.
Main side runs are party at 18°C by default. Rear neighbour-side contact remains unresolved; call choices and their effects are recorded separately.
Basement exposed walls assumed 30% air / 70% ground at 10°C; openings outside.
Cool basement is an imposed 11°C boundary hypothesis, not an equilibrium calculation.
Photo-based radiator outputs are catalogue analogues with broad size/type ranges, not measurements; inventories and some room attributions are incomplete.
Thermal bridges use an explicit 0.05–0.15 W/m²K envelope allowance.

Running costs use an explicit annual-heat proxy and assumed seasonal efficiencies. BUS is an assumed deduction, not confirmed eligibility. Equipment performance and regulatory approval remain unverified.
